catalog_quote: [Nevin p.60] Syllables may have high or low pitch or tone, marked as acute accent vs. null over the vowel, e.g. /á/ vs. /a/, as in these two monosyllabic words: 48. áp "mouth" 49. as "water" A few cases of falling tone are analyzed in the usual way, as high tone followed by low tone on successive vowels in a vowel cluster. [p.58] Lax vowels and [ə] are always in unstressed syllables. Any of the lax vowels may be made tense if stressed, as for example in careful citation of isolated words. [p.94] There is, however, a complication in the data. A glottal stop may optionally be inserted, especially if the following syllable is stressed: 92. qa ʔáp ~ qa áp "the mouth" 93. qá ʔas ~ qá as "the water" 94. dáx slaʔám ~ dáx slaám "What shall I eat?" Stress and pitch are independent, as is shown in (93). A glottal stop can sometimes be heard even before an unstressed syllable, especially in careful pronunciation of isolated citation forms: 95. ʔaj·át ~ aj·át "ground squirrel" [de Angulo & Freeland 1930 p.80] Pitch-tone. Pitch-tone is extremely important in Achumawi. There are two main tones: high, and low. The difference in pitch between them is about that of a fourth. [Uldall 1933 sec.4] Achumawi is a tone language, i.e. differences in pitch-tone are distinctive semantically and, to a certain extent, morphologically. There are two tonemes, a high, level tone and a low, level one; proper rising or falling tones do not occur

new_statements.rule_in_words: Achumawi is described as having lexical high vs. low pitch (tone) on every syllable; stress is mentioned as a separate parameter that is independent of pitch (an unstressed syllable can bear high pitch and vice versa) and that conditions vowel laxing and optional glottal-stop insertion, but the source gives no rule for which syllable of a word is stressed. The two earlier first-hand descriptions (de Angulo & Freeland 1930:80; Uldall 1933:76) likewise treat Achumawi as a pitch-tone language with two level tonemes plus contrastive length and say nothing about word stress (de Angulo & Freeland explicitly contrast Achumawi pitch-tone with the incipient 'stress accent' of Atsugewi and Shasta).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress placement; Nevin notes reduced stress on the auxiliary duji in certain syntactic environments causes final-syllable devoicing (p.30-31 of ch.1 discussion of Uldall), and utterance-final devoicing/whisper in downriver dialects.
new_statements.domain_note: Pitch is per syllable (word-level lexical tone). The stress remarks concern phonetic realization in phrases (qa + noun) and in careful citation of isolated words; no word-domain stress rule is formulated.
new_statements.identity_note: All three first-hand sources describe Achumawi proper (achu1247, language level). de Angulo & Freeland 1930 and Uldall 1933 record mainly the upriver dialect around Alturas (Qosalektawi band, per Voegelin 1946:98 n.7); Nevin 1998 worked 1970-74 and 1990s with speakers of several bands (up- and downriver) and notes dialect differences only in voicing and utterance-final devoicing, not prosody. Atsugewi (atsu1245), the sister language, is explicitly said by de Angulo & Freeland to be shifting toward stress accent -- that remark must not be attributed to Achumawi.

new_statements.quote: Length (C· and V·) is contrastive in both languages. Achumawi has contrastive high and low pitch; a stressed syllable with low pitch may occur next to an unstressed syllable with high pitch. Atsugewi has a stress system. In some classes of Achumawi verbs, pitch and length are largely predictable, apparently an earlier stress pattern, but Achumawi high pitch and Atsugewi stress typically do not fall on the corresponding syllables: [Achumawi : Atsugewi example pairs glossed 'bird (generic)' and 'crested bluejay'; italic vernacular forms not decodable]. [p.20 fn.25:] Harrington did not record contrastive pitch—an acute accent may mark a perception of stress—

new_statements.rule_in_words: Achumawi (Pit River) has a lexical high/low pitch contrast, and stress is independent of pitch (a stressed low-pitched syllable can sit next to an unstressed high-pitched one); in some verb classes pitch and length are largely predictable, which Nevin reads as the residue of an earlier stress pattern. No rule for where Achumawi stress falls is given. The sister language Atsugewi, by contrast, 'has a stress system', and its stress does not fall on the syllables that carry Achumawi high pitch.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the remark that in some classes of Achumawi verbs pitch and length are largely predictable ('apparently an earlier stress pattern'); p. 12 notes high pitch is written with an acute accent (replacing Olmsted's macron); fn. 25 (p. 20) warns that Harrington's acute accents may record perceived stress rather than pitch.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are about Achumawi proper (ISO acv; Nevin's own 1970-74/1992 fieldwork database, upriver and downriver varieties pooled). Nevin 2019 sec. 2 sketches Achumawi and Atsugewi side by side; the sentence 'Atsugewi has a stress system' belongs to Atsugewi (atsu1245) and must not be filed under achu1247.
